record.paper_title: Open Questions in CMR Manganites, Relevance of Clustered States, and Analogies with other Compounds
record.original_question: Are the glassy states observed in some manganites ordinary spin glasses or a distinct class of phase-separated glasses or cluster glasses, how should such glasses be classified, and what time-dependent phenomena are essential for determining their nature?

evidence.quote: Is the glassy state in some manganites of the same variety as a standard spin-glass, or does it belong to a new class of "phase-separated glasses"? ... Can glasses be classified into different groups? Are glassy manganites a new class? What is the actual nature of the "cluster glasses" frequently mentioned in manganites? ... Studies of time-dependent phenomena in the x=0.5 regime has provided fascinating results, that deserve further research.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider hole-doped manganite compounds of the form R_{1-x}A_x MnO_3 (with R a trivalent rare-earth ion and A a divalent alkaline-earth ion) in regimes where neutron, transport, and magnetization measurements reveal coexisting ferromagnetic metallic and antiferromagnetic/charge-ordered insulating regions on nanometer to micrometer length scales. At low temperatures, many such systems exhibit "glassy" magnetic behavior: history dependence, memory and aging effects, slow non-exponential relaxation of the magnetization, frequency-dependent peaks in the ac susceptibility, and a divergence of relaxation times resembling that of canonical spin glasses (e.g., dilute magnetic alloys such as CuMn) or cluster glasses (interacting frozen ferromagnetic clusters).

Formulate and resolve the following:

(a) Establish criteria, based on equilibrium and non-equilibrium magnetic observables (e.g., scaling of the nonlinear susceptibility chi_3 near a freezing temperature T_f, critical exponents of a putative spin-glass transition, aging and memory protocols, thermo-remanent and isothermal remanent magnetization decay, and noise/fluctuation–dissipation behavior), that distinguish a canonical atomic spin glass from a phase-separated glass whose elementary degrees of freedom are mesoscopic clusters of correlated spins/charges.

(b) Determine whether the glassy low-temperature states observed in representative phase-separated manganites (in particular near half-doping x ≈ 0.5, where charge/orbital ordering competes with ferromagnetism) fall into the universality class of standard Heisenberg/Ising spin glasses, or whether they constitute a genuinely distinct class — to be called "phase-separated glasses" or "cluster glasses" — characterized by frozen-in inhomogeneity of coexisting electronic phases rather than by frustrated atomic exchange interactions.

(c) Provide a classification of magnetic glassy states that includes (i) canonical spin glasses, (ii) cluster glasses with well-defined ferromagnetic clusters, and (iii) phase-separated electronic glasses with competing ordered phases, specifying which time-dependent phenomena (aging, rejuvenation, memory, sub-aging exponents, waiting-time dependence of relaxation, breakdown of the fluctuation–dissipation theorem) are essential diagnostics for assigning a given material to one of these classes.
artifact.status_search_result: Recent literature continues to debate whether glassy manganite states are canonical spin glasses or distinct cluster/phase-separated glasses. Studies on Nd2/3Ca1/3MnO3, Eu0.5Ba0.5MnO3, and La2/3Sr1/3-based systems report cluster-glass and Griffiths-phase signatures with both similarities and contradictions to conventional spin glasses, and a general classification has not been settled.

status_evidence.title: Critical exponents and the correlation length in the manganite spin glass Eu0.5Ba0.5MnO3
status_evidence.snippet: Studies of critical exponents in manganite spin-glass-like systems show similarities and contradictions with conventional spin glasses.
status_evidence.claim: The universality class of manganite glassy states relative to canonical spin glasses is still under active investigation.

status_evidence.title: Evidence for a Griffiths Phase to Cluster Spin Glass Transition in La2/3Sr1/3(Mn1-3xAl2xTix)O3
status_evidence.snippet: Recent work identifies cluster spin glass behavior emerging from a Griffiths phase in substituted manganites.
status_evidence.claim: Cluster-glass versus canonical spin-glass classification in manganites remains an active research topic.

status_evidence.title: Cluster glass magnetism in the phase-separated Nd2/3Ca1/3MnO3 perovskite
status_evidence.snippet: Phase-separated manganite shows cluster glass magnetism distinct from atomic spin glasses.
status_evidence.claim: Phase-separated glasses in manganites are reported but a unified classification is not established.
